answer.rationale: memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory: it is the only record supporting the one direction that can satisfy an 18% mandate the incumbent has refused to reopen (memory_c4's renegotiation lever and memory_c6's multi-year lever are both foreclosed this cycle by that refusal; memory_c5's defer path is unavailable because the contract does not auto-renew and the line has no buffer). So I spend the single verification pull on memory_c2 rather than on memories whose recommended actions are already blocked. What I need from the archive is specifically what memory_c2 does NOT claim: it attests to unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy — it says nothing about on-time delivery performance at or near committed volume, nothing about behavior under allocation stress, and it is a year old, so the vendor's capacity position may have changed. Those are exactly the dimensions that matter at 94% utilization with zero buffer. Downstream risk: a full primary switch in 14 days would convert a cost problem into a single-point-of-failure delivery problem, and memory_c3 is the standing warning that removing redundancy on a constrained component is what hurt us before — a wholesale move to one unproven-at-volume vendor recreates that exposure in mirror image, and any later agent inheriting a 'switch worked' record would compound it. Therefore: commit to the switch as the direction, but execute as a small guarded test — qualify the low-cost vendor on a carved-out share of volume with the incumbent's supply bridged short-term, staged release gates on measured on-time delivery, and an explicit rollback. If the archive shows memory_c2's cost win came from a period of slack demand or without delivery-reliability evidence, the guarded scale is what keeps that gap from becoming a line stoppage; if it shows verified at-volume performance, the staged gates retire quickly and the mandate is met next review. I am not treating the 18% mandate as satisfied by a quote alone.
